passage: Kashish sat on the charpai in Leela's courtyard in a small Rajasthan town, sipping tea while Leela's father spread three photographs on the cot. "This boy has a house and a steady shop. No bad habits, good family," he said, tapping each one. "When Chotu's daughter's match broke, the whole street talked for a year. I won't have that for Leela." His hands shook slightly as he straightened the pictures. Leela's mother kept refilling glasses. Leela herself looked at the gate and said only, "Papa, my diploma ends in March." Her father nodded and went on about the shop. Kashish, Leela's friend since school, felt her chest tighten. She could see how much he loved his daughter, and how little of the plan had asked her.

qa.q: How many photographs did Leela's father spread on the cot?
qa.a: He spread three photographs on the cot.

qa.q: What is Kashish feeling as she watches Leela's father?
qa.a: Kashish feels torn and worried. She sees his love for his daughter, but her chest tightens because Leela has not been asked what she wants.

qa.q: What could Kashish choose to do after the visit to help both Leela and Leela's father?
qa.a: Kashish could encourage Leela to tell her father calmly what she wants, such as finishing her diploma, and gently suggest that Leela's own view belongs in a safe, respectable match.

qa.q: Why might Leela's father hurry with the photographs?
qa.a: He fears the street talking for a year if a match breaks, as it did for Chotu's daughter. He hurries out of care and worry, even though he is not yet listening to Leela.

grounding: A friend sees a girl's parents searching for a safe, respectable match out of care and fear of gossip, without yet asking her what she wants.

passage: Lunch break at the bakery in Rosario, and Pablo's phone buzzed for the third time. Ivan, cutting rolls beside him, heard Pablo's half of it: "Mamá, I know she's a doctor's daughter... yes, from a good family... no, I'm not saying no, I'm saying slowly." After hanging up, Pablo rubbed his forehead. "She has a list. Safe job, respected surname, someone the church ladies will approve of. A neighbour's daughter's marriage fell apart last year and half the barrio whispered." Ivan noticed that Pablo never said a bad word about his mother. Ivan also noticed that Pablo hadn't said what he himself hoped for. "What do you want?" Ivan asked. Pablo laughed, surprised. "Nobody's asked me that yet."

qa.q: Where is the bakery?
qa.a: The bakery is in Rosario.

qa.q: What does Ivan notice about Pablo that shows how Pablo feels toward his mother?
qa.a: Pablo never says a bad word about her, which suggests he loves her and understands her fear, though he is stuck between her plan and his own unspoken hopes.

qa.q: What turning point came when Ivan asked "What do you want?"
qa.a: It gave Pablo a chance to say what he himself wants, which nobody had asked, and could lead to a fuller talk with his mother.

qa.q: How might Pablo's mother see the search for a match?
qa.a: As care. She wants someone safe and respected, and fears the barrio whispering, as it did when a neighbour's daughter's marriage fell apart.

grounding: A bystander overhears one side of a parent's call about a safe, respectable match, sees care behind it, and notices the young person's own wishes are unspoken.

passage:
The matrimonial bureau was on the second floor of the community hall, above a tailor's shop. Kunal sat between his parents on a plastic bench while Ojas, the young clerk, scrolled through profiles on a desktop.
"Government job preferred," Papa said. "Stable. Safe."
"And a good family. People talk if anything goes wrong," Mummy added, lowering her voice as if the neighbours were in the next room.
Kunal watched Papa's knee bounce. Papa had been laid off twice in the nineties; Kunal remembered the silence at dinner those years. So that was what "stable" meant.
Ojas asked, "What does Kunal want?"
Both parents turned, as if surprised the question existed.
Kunal said, "Someone I can talk to." Mummy squeezed his hand, and her eyes were wet, but she also asked Ojas to filter by salary.

qa.q: Where was the matrimonial bureau?
qa.a: The matrimonial bureau was on the second floor of the community hall, above a tailor's shop.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he watched Papa's knee bounce?
qa.a: Kunal felt a sad understanding, even sympathy; remembering Papa's layoffs, he saw that Papa's wish for a stable match came from old fear.

qa.q: How could Kunal help his parents hear what he wants?
qa.a: He could talk to them at home, thank them for caring about safety, and explain what "someone I can talk to" means to him, so their worry and his wish are both heard.

qa.q: How does Mummy seem to see the search?
qa.a: Mummy is torn: she is moved by Kunal's answer, but her fear of what people will say still makes her ask Ojas to filter by salary.

grounding: An adult child observes his parents' search for a safe, respectable match, seeing both their caring motives and their blindness to his wishes.

passage:
Hi Asif,
Sorry for the silence. It's been a strange month at home.
My parents are looking for a match for my sister Mercy. I've been watching from the sidelines, and it's harder than I expected. Appa checks every family's income twice. Amma asks the church aunties about each boy's mother, because she's scared Mercy will go somewhere unkind.
Last week they found a "perfect" family. Mercy said she wasn't sure, and Amma said, "What will people think if we refuse such a proposal?" Mercy went quiet. I saw her face and thought, nobody has asked what she wants from her life.
I don't think my parents are wrong to worry. Appa grew up with very little. But I'm worried the worry is choosing for her.
I'm going to talk to Appa this weekend, just the two of us. Any advice?
Joseph

qa.q: Whom does Amma ask about each boy's mother?
qa.a: Amma asks the church aunties about each boy's mother.

qa.q: What is Joseph worried about as he watches his family?
qa.a: Joseph is worried that the parents' fear is choosing for Mercy, and Joseph feels uneasy that nobody has asked what she wants.

qa.q: What could Joseph say to Appa this weekend?
qa.a: Joseph could first acknowledge that Appa's care comes from growing up with little, then gently ask him to sit down with Mercy and hear what she wants.

qa.q: How might Mercy feel when Amma asks what people will think?
qa.a: Mercy may feel silenced and pressured, as if the community's opinion counts more than her own doubts about the match.

grounding: A sibling watching from the sidelines writes about parents seeking a safe, respectable match out of care, and fearing talk, while missing what his sister wants.

passage:
Keerthana, you'll laugh, but last night I sat on the stairs and listened to my parents discuss my wedding like a budget meeting.
Appa said, "He must have his own flat. I don't want Arohi struggling like we did." Amma said, "And the family should be decent. If it breaks, the whole street will know." Then Appa said, very softly, "I just want her safe."
I sat there with my chin on my knees. I felt so loved, honestly. And also invisible. Nobody said, "Arohi wants to do her PhD." Nobody said, "Arohi hates big cities."
This morning I made them filter coffee and said, "Can I be in the next meeting about me?" Amma laughed, then stopped when she saw my face. She said, "Okay. Sunday."
So that's the story, Keerthana. I'm Arohi, and on Sunday I get a chair at my own wedding meeting.

qa.q: Where did Arohi sit last night?
qa.a: Arohi sat on the stairs and listened to her parents discuss her wedding.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Arohi have on the stairs?
qa.a: Arohi felt loved, because Appa said he just wanted her safe, and also invisible, because nobody mentioned her PhD or that she hates big cities.

qa.q: Which step did Arohi take, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She made coffee and calmly asked to join the next meeting about her; that honoured her parents' care while making room for her own wishes.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when she stopped laughing?
qa.a: Amma may have felt surprised and a little moved, realising that Arohi was serious about being part of decisions about her own life.

grounding: An adult daughter overhears her parents seek a safe, well-off, respectable match out of care and fear of talk, and notices they have left out her wishes.

passage:
I'm Chaitanya, Samir's cousin, and I've been watching his parents hunt for a bride all year. I don't know what's truly in their hearts, only what I see. Every Sunday Chachi spreads biodatas on the dining table and sorts them into piles: good family, good job, "respectable". Chacha phones people to ask about each girl's father. Last month he rejected one because her parents were divorced. "What will people say?" he said, rubbing his forehead.
Samir sits there with his guitar case by the door. He tells them he wants someone who likes music, who laughs. Chachi pats his hand. "Music doesn't pay rent, beta." I see how tired she looks, how often she checks her phone for replies. They love him, obviously. They want him safe. But I can see Samir going quieter each Sunday. Last week he didn't even come downstairs.

qa.q: Why did Chacha reject one girl last month?
qa.a: Because her parents were divorced.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya feel watching the Sunday biodata sorting?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels uneasy and a bit sad, seeing both the parents' love and Samir growing quieter.

qa.q: What could Samir's parents try so they see what he wants?
qa.a: They could sit with Samir and ask what matters most to him, and include qualities like music and laughter alongside safety and family.

qa.q: How does Chachi see the search for a bride?
qa.a: She sees it as caring for Samir, wanting him safe and settled, while feeling tired and anxious, checking her phone for replies.

grounding: It illustrates an observer who sees parents seek a safe, respectable match out of care and fear of talk, while missing what the young man wants.
